## February 29, 1960 — A Monday

Before anything else: you were born on a day that does not exist in most years. February 29th arrives once every four years, and you arrived on one of those rare Mondays. Chronologically you are sixty-six years old. In terms of actual birthdays — the date itself appearing on a calendar — you have had sixteen. The next one comes in 2028. There is no other fact about your birthdate that matches this one for sheer peculiarity. You share it with a very small cohort of humans across history, bound together by nothing except the stubbornness of the Gregorian calendar's arithmetic.

---

**A city was destroyed the night you were born.** In the early hours of February 29, 1960, an earthquake struck Agadir, Morocco — a compact coastal city whose buildings were largely earthen and unbraced. The magnitude was moderate by seismic standards, but the destruction was near-total. Somewhere between twelve and fifteen thousand people died, roughly a third of the city's population, in a matter of seconds. Agadir was essentially erased. The news reached the world on the morning of your birth. It was one of the defining catastrophes of 1960, and 1960 had no shortage of them.

**The sit-in movement was twenty-eight days old.** On February 1st — four weeks before you were born — four Black college students sat down at a Woolworth's lunch counter in Greensboro, North Carolina and refused to leave when denied service. By February 29th, the movement they sparked had spread to dozens of cities across the South. You were born on the twenty-ninth day of what became the student phase of the Civil Rights Movement — the moment young people stepped to the front. The Civil Rights Act came when you were four. The Voting Rights Act when you were five. The revolution that began four weeks before your birth defined the America you grew up in.

**You were born in the last year of one world and the first year of another.** Dwight Eisenhower was still president when you arrived. By the time you were nine months old, John F. Kennedy had been elected. The transition from Eisenhower's America to Kennedy's was more than political — it was a shift in tone, generation, and possibility that the country felt viscerally. You have no memory of Eisenhower's America. Kennedy's is where your consciousness begins.

**1960 was the Year of Africa.** The year of your birth was when the map of the world was redrawn more rapidly than at any point since the end of the Second World War. Seventeen African nations achieved independence in 1960 alone — Congo, Nigeria, Senegal, Ivory Coast, Cameroon, and a dozen more, in a cascade that spanned the entire year. The colonial order that had organized the world for a century was visibly collapsing. You were born into the first year of the post-colonial world, though that world would take decades more to define itself.

**The birth control pill was approved four months after your birth.** The FDA approved oral contraceptives in June 1960. The social transformation that followed — the renegotiation of women's lives, careers, families, and autonomy — unfolded across your childhood and adolescence. You grew up in the first generation for which that transformation was not a revolution in progress but a settled, if contested, background condition.

**The leap day itself is a calendar anomaly with a human cost.** Julius Caesar's astronomers added the intercalary day; Pope Gregory XIII's reform refined it. The February 29 that produced your birthday has existed only because of two separate decisions by two different empires about how to reconcile the solar year with the calendar year. Most people's birthdays are accidents of biology. Yours is also an accident of Roman and Renaissance astronomy.

---

**The arc of a lifetime.**

You are sixty-six years old as of this year, 2026, but you have marked that in only sixteen calendar ceremonies where the actual date cooperated.

You were three when Kennedy was assassinated. Nine when Armstrong walked on the moon. Fourteen when Nixon resigned. Twenty-nine when the Berlin Wall came down — old enough to understand exactly what it meant, young enough to feel the future opening rather than closing.

The internet arrived in your mid-thirties. The smartphone in your late forties. COVID at sixty. You have watched the world change at a pace that no previous generation experienced and that future generations may not experience again, because the transformations of 1960 to 2026 — in medicine, communication, geopolitics, and daily life — are of a density that may not be repeatable.

Born on a day that barely exists, in a year that was the hinge of the twentieth century, into a world that was simultaneously mourning Agadir, watching the sit-ins spread, electing its youngest president, and redrawing the map of an entire continent. Sixty-six years of ordinary and extraordinary life, measured sixteen times by the date that made you unusual from the start.
